title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Christian Religious Studies Second Term covers (new life, sonship, faith and works, the Spirit, forgiveness and humility) and a map of every unit.

p: In First Term you studied who Jesus is and how God loves us. In Second Term you study how a person who follows Jesus should live. The topics are New Life in Christ, Sonship, Faith and Works, the Fruit of the Spirit, Spiritual Gifts, Forgiveness and Humility. They help you to build character, which matters in school, at home and in every exam question on Christian living.

Read the Bible texts first, then the notes. Each unit ends with practice questions that do not count towards a mark; they help you to see whether you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit. Write the main verse of each unit in your notebook and one action you will take.

title: New Life in Christ
summary: What new life means, baptism as a picture of burial and resurrection, putting off vices and putting on virtues, steps and challenges, and the work of the Holy Spirit.

p: Read 2 Corinthians 5:17; Colossians 3:1-17; Romans 6:3-4; John 3:1-5. New life in Christ is a spiritual change that happens when someone accepts Jesus as personal Lord and Saviour. Character, values and priorities change. It is a 'dying' to sin and a beginning to live in righteousness by the power of the Holy Spirit. 'If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away; behold, the new has come.'

Paul teaches that baptism is a public sign of union with Christ. When a believer goes under the water by immersion it pictures being buried with Christ, and the old self dies. Coming up from the water pictures rising with Christ to a new life. Baptism is a symbol: a person can be baptised and not have a changed heart, so the ritual must go with a real change of heart.

Paul uses the picture of changing clothes: take off the dirty clothes and put on clean ones. Put off vices: anger, rage, malice, slander, filthy language, lying, sexual immorality and evil desires. Put on virtues: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness and love (which binds everything together in unity). Let the peace of Christ rule in your heart and set your mind on things above.

Steps: hear God's word, confess sin, repent and be baptised, and decide to live like Christ and join the body of believers. The new life cannot be lived by willpower alone. The Holy Spirit empowers us to resist sin, guides us into truth (John 14:26) and produces spiritual fruit.

Expect challenges: temptation from peers and the world, ridicule for being different, and struggles with old habits. The rewards are assurance of salvation, peace with God and people, and God's guidance. We become new at once when we are saved, but our minds are renewed every day.

activity: Write one page: 'How I can live the new life in Christ as a student.' Include changes in study habits, language and relationships.

title: Sonship: Children and Heirs of God
summary: Creation and adoption, the cry 'Abba, Father', Paul's picture of a child heir, unity in Christ, and the duties of a child of God.

p: Read Romans 8:14-17 and Galatians 3:26-4:7. In one sense all people are God's creatures because He made them. But the Bible speaks of a special status, sonship, which is a relationship. Through Adam's disobedience people lost the closeness of being God's children and became estranged. Jesus came and obeyed perfectly so that people can be brought back into God's family.

Paul uses the legal word adoption. In Roman law an adopted son had exactly the same rights as a natural son. God sends the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, and we cry 'Abba! Father!' Abba is an Aramaic word of closeness, like 'Daddy' or 'Papa'. It shows a relationship of love, not fear. The word 'son' here speaks of legal standing and inheritance and applies to women as well as men.

Paul pictures a child who is heir but, while still a minor, is treated like a slave under guardians. Before Christ, people were under strict rules. 'When the fullness of time had come', God sent His Son to redeem those under the law, so we receive adoption. We are no longer slaves but sons, and if sons, then heirs.

In God's family, earthly differences disappear: 'There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ.' Those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs of the promise.

Led by the Spirit: 'All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.' Obedience: as Jesus obeyed the Father, sons obey and do their duties, civic and spiritual. Disobedience hurts fellowship with the Father. Kingdom work: sons share the Gospel and give their 'quota in cash and kind' to support its spread.
Summary: past, slaves to fear and the law; present, adopted children who cry 'Abba, Father'; future, heirs with Christ.

activity: Read Galatians 4:7. Write a letter to God beginning 'Abba, Father' and thank Him for three blessings you have as His child.

title: Faith and Works
summary: What faith and works are, the mirror picture, James' three arguments, how Paul and James agree, and practical religion.

p: Read James 1:22-27 and 2:14-26. Faith means trust: not only agreeing with facts but trusting God and accepting that Jesus died and rose for me. Works are faith shown in practical action. Works are the visible proof of invisible faith, as smoke shows that there is fire.

A person who only hears the word is like a man who looks in a mirror, sees his dirty face, walks away and forgets what he looks like. He deceives himself. The doer looks into the perfect law of liberty and acts on it, and is blessed.

Faith without works is dead. 1. The demons: 'Even the demons believe, and shudder.' They accept that God exists, but they do not submit. Believing God exists is not enough. 2. Abraham: he was shown to be right by his obedience when he offered Isaac. His faith was 'completed' by what he did. 3. The body: 'As the body apart from the spirit is dead, so faith apart from works is dead.'

Paul says we are saved by faith (Ephesians 2:8); James says faith without works is dead. They fight different enemies. Paul fights legalism, the idea that we can earn heaven by good deeds, and stresses the root of salvation: faith. James fights laziness, the idea that we can live in sin and still say we believe, and stresses the fruit of salvation: works. We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone.
Pure religion (James 1:27): to visit orphans and widows in their trouble, which is care for the vulnerable, and to keep oneself unstained by the world, which is moral purity.

activity: Faith in Action: this week do one specific kind act for a person in need at school or in your neighbourhood. Write how it 'completed' your faith.

title: The Fruit of the Spirit
summary: The meaning of fruit, love as the root of the nine attributes, works of the flesh against fruit of the Spirit, and how fruit is produced.

p: Read Galatians 5:19-25. Fruit is the natural produce of a plant. It carries seeds and gives food. The fruit of the Spirit means the lasting qualities of a good Christian, the visible sign that God's light is in a believer. Paul says 'fruit' in the singular, so the nine qualities are one cluster, not nine separate items. It is hard to have patience without love or peace without self-control.

Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Love is the root: joy is love rejoicing, peace is love resting, patience is love enduring, kindness is love serving. A person with no love lacks the whole fruit.

Paul contrasts the fruit with the works of the flesh. The flesh produces 'works', which are effort and struggle; the Spirit produces 'fruit', which is natural growth. The works of the flesh include sexual sins (adultery, fornication, uncleanness), religious sins (idolatry, witchcraft) and social sins (hatred, strife, jealousy, anger, selfish ambition, envy, murder, drunkenness). People who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God.

Fruit cannot be forced; it must grow. First, salvation: confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised Him (Romans 10:9-10). Second, the Holy Spirit living in you, as at Pentecost when tongues of fire rested on the disciples (Acts 2:3-8). Gifts show God's power; fruit shows God's character. A tree is known by its fruit, and a Christian is known by love, patience and self-control, not by how loudly he prays.

title: Spiritual Gifts
summary: Gifts compared with talents, the nine gifts in three groups, how they are given, and why: the common good and unity in the one body.

p: Read 1 Corinthians 12:1-11; Ephesians 4:11-13; Romans 12:3-8. Spiritual gifts are special abilities that the Holy Spirit gives to believers for service. They are for building up the church and for God's mission, not for personal gain.

Talents are natural or learned skills such as singing, drawing or mathematics. Spiritual gifts are given by the Spirit for spiritual service. Both should be used for God's glory, with humility: 'think with sober judgment' (Romans 12:3).

Revelation gifts (they 'know'): word of wisdom (insight into what to do), word of knowledge (insight into facts and truths of the faith) and discerning of spirits (telling whether a spiritual action is from God, an evil spirit or a human spirit).
Power gifts (they 'do'): faith (bold, mountain-moving trust), gifts of healing and working of miracles.
Utterance gifts (they 'speak'): prophecy (speaking God's message to encourage, strengthen and comfort, which is not only foretelling), speaking in tongues and interpretation of tongues.

They all come from one Spirit. Every believer has at least one gift. The Spirit gives them 'as He wills', so we cannot demand a gift. They are for the common good: the church is like a body where the hand needs the eye, so no one person has every gift and we depend on one another. Using our gifts helps us to resist the world's pattern, to be changed, and to fulfil our calling.
The Corinthian church had many gifts but was immature. Having gifts does not prove maturity; having the fruit of the Spirit does. The aim is a united, mature church where each part does its work.

activity: Write a paragraph on a gift you admire or think you may have. How would you use it to help a group in your school?

title: Forgiveness: The Story of Philemon and Onesimus
summary: What forgiveness means, Paul's letter to Philemon as a model of mediation, three ways forgiveness comes, and what unforgiveness does.

p: Read Matthew 6:14-15 and 18:21-35 and the letter to Philemon. To forgive is to have no further wish to punish someone for an offence: letting go of ill feeling and the desire for revenge. God took the first step in restoring us when we were sinners, and Christians are to restore offenders in the same way. Jesus says that if we do not forgive others, our Father will not forgive us. There is no limit: 'seventy times seven' means a lifestyle of forgiving.

Philemon was a wealthy Christian in Colossae who led a church in his house. Onesimus, his slave, ran away to Rome. Under Roman law a runaway slave could be put to death. In Rome Onesimus met Paul, who was in prison, and became a Christian.

Paul did not use his authority to give orders. He appealed in love. He sent Onesimus back 'no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother'. The name Onesimus means 'useful': once useless to Philemon, he was now useful to both. Paul even offered to pay any debt: 'If he has wronged you or owes you anything, charge that to my account' (verse 18), which is like Jesus taking our debt. Paul's goal was full reconciliation and restored brotherhood.

Repentance: the offender admits wrong and asks for pardon. Unconditional mercy: the offended person, moved by God's love, forgives even without an apology. Mediation: a third person, like Paul, brings the two sides together.

Emotional: hatred and bitterness grow. Social: war, lack of peace and disunity in families and communities. Spiritual: slow growth and hindered prayer. Christians should be peacemakers, obey God by forgiving, and help offenders to find their place again, as Onesimus was restored.

Note: forgiving does not always mean trusting immediately (for example after theft), but it does mean giving up the wish to punish. Some traditions say Onesimus later became a church leader, but this is not certain.

activity: Think of a conflict, past or present. Write a 'letter of mediation' as if Paul were advising you on how to handle it, using the ideas from Philemon.

title: Humility
summary: What humility is, the mind of Christ in Philippians 2, Peter's teaching on humility and anxiety, and expressions of humility in daily life.

p: Humility is a state of mind that holds a modest opinion of oneself. It is the opposite of pride. It means knowing that we depend on God and valuing others above ourselves. It is one of the greatest marks of a Christian and brings understanding, progress, peace and harmony.

Paul wrote to a church in Philippi that was divided; the root causes were selfishness and a lack of humility. He pointed to Jesus. Jesus was 'in the form of God' and equal with God. He did not hold on to this for His own gain. He emptied Himself (the word kenosis), took the form of a servant, was born as a man, and became obedient even to death on a cross.

Because He went to the lowest place, God lifted Him to the highest. 'God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name,' so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. The way up is down.

Peter tells young people to be submissive to their elders, and all to 'clothe yourselves with humility'. 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.' If you humble yourself under God's hand, He will lift you up in due time: promotion comes from God, not self-promotion.

Humility and worry: 'Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.' Worry can be a form of pride, thinking we must solve everything ourselves. Peter also warns that the devil prowls like a roaring lion; we resist him by being sober, watchful and firm in faith.

Serving without seeking applause. Forgiving readily. Obeying rules and lawful authority. Putting the community's good above personal gain. True humility is not hiding your talents. Jesus knew He was God and chose to serve. Humility is using your strength to serve others, not to dominate them.

activity: Write a paragraph on a leader in history or in your community who showed humility, and how it helped them to bring peace or success.
